definition: Morning-after headache, nausea and regret. Fancy name: veisalgia. Water and time help; no hangover cure beats the second-last drink.
A patient’s record. Paper ones used to hang at the end of the hospital bed.
Saddle-shaped hollow in the skull base that holds the pituitary (sella turcica).
Reflex that clears the airways.
Largest internal organ. Processes nutrients, makes bile, clears drugs and toxins.
Large intestine. Absorbs water and forms stool.
Break in skin or mucous membrane that fails to heal.
Inflamed small intestine, usually from a bug like norovirus: the ‘gastro’ behind vomiting and diarrhoea. Small, frequent sips of oral rehydration solution beat sports drinks.
Fleshy tag hanging from the back of the soft palate.
Notch where vessels and nerves enter an organ such as the lung or kidney.
Bundle of fibres carrying signals between the brain and body.
The team’s daily visit to every patient on the ward. Juniors write very fast.
Gas escaping from the stomach. Fizzy drinks and eating quickly cause more of them.
Organ that makes and releases substances such as hormones.
As in psammoma bodies: tiny layered calcium specks seen down the microscope in papillary thyroid cancer, meningioma and serous ovarian tumours. Greek psammos, sand.
The visible outer ear flap.
Chalky urate deposits under the skin in chronic gout.
Cooling fluid from skin glands. Palms and soles have the most glands.
Living tissue that is constantly rebuilt. Your skeleton is replaced roughly every ten years.
Shin bone. The larger of the two lower-leg bones.
A viral infection that swells the salivary glands by the jaw. Vaccines made it rare.
The science of hearing and balance; audiologists test hearing and fit aids and implants. The multichannel cochlear implant was pioneered in Melbourne by Graeme Clark’s team, first implanted in 1978.
The nostrils.
Unit of magnetic field strength. Most MRI scanners run at 1.5 or 3 of them.
Bones of the head that protect the brain.
A test of a treatment in people. The randomised controlled trial is the gold standard.
A virus that can paralyse. Vaccination has cut cases by more than 99%.
Itchy, raised welts (urticaria), often from an allergy or infection.

Chlamydial eye infection that scars the eyelids and can blind. Australia is the only high-income country where it’s still endemic, in some remote Aboriginal communities. Clean faces and safe water help end it.
A rounded mass of chewed food, or a single large dose of a drug.
Newborn score out of 10, checked at 1 and 5 minutes after birth.
